summary: A 1973 memo reporting what a small informal meeting at UCLA concluded about the ARPANET File Transfer Protocol. It covers transfers between two remote servers, site-dependent information, and nitpicks about earlier FTP proposals (RFC 354, 385 and 414). It is a discussion paper, not a specification.

eli5.summary: Some people who build file-sending programs met in a room and wrote down what they agreed and disagreed about, so everyone could fix the rules together.

questions: what is the ftp getsocket command
subtitle: Notes from a January 1973 UCLA meeting on FTP: server-to-server transfers, type encoding and site-specific parameters.

tldr.problem: FTP as described in RFC 354, RFC 385 and RFC 414 had unclear points, no way for two servers to exchange files directly, and no place for host-specific file parameters.
tldr.mechanism: R. Braden reports the meeting's consensus on server-server transfers, site-dependent information and miscellaneous disagreements, and proposes multi-letter TYPE codes and a GETSocket command.
tldr.outcome: The RFC endorses the general model of RFC 438 for server-server transfer and describes CCN's plan to handle IBM file-system parameters through keywords on the pathname.

sections.title: The January 1973 FTP Meeting
sections.content:
On January 23, 1973, Jon Postel (NMC), Eric Harslem (RAND), Stephen Wolfe (CCN) and Robert Braden (CCN) held an informal meeting at UCLA on FTP. This RFC reports its general consensus on server-server transfers (see RFC 438 by Thomas and Clements), site-dependent information, and miscellaneous disagreements with RFC 354, RFC 385 and RFC 414.

The "print file muddle" was also discussed but is covered in a separate RFC, RFC 448.
sections.eli5: Four people met to sort out disagreements about the file-sending rules, and this note reports what they decided.

sections.title: Miscellaneous Comments and Type Encoding
sections.content:
The comments include a view that some items in earlier RFCs are unnecessary concessions to bad implementations. An implementation relying on "immediately after" in an asynchronous multi-process system like the ARPA Network is called erroneous. Other notes: there is no way in FTP to change a password, and the order of sending TYPE before BYTE should be a recommendation for user FTP, not a restriction on servers.

On type encoding, the RFC observes that the print file attribute is independent of the character code, so FTP has at least four character types. It proposes multi-character TYPE codes: A for ASCII, E for EBCDIC, P for print file, I for image and L for local byte, giving A, AP, E, EP, I and L. Text mode is not possible for EBCDIC files, but stream and block modes work.
sections.eli5: They point out small mistakes and propose spelling file types with several letters, like building words from parts, so new kinds can be added later.

sections.title: Server-Server Interaction
sections.content:
RFC 438 proposed that a controller process connect to two server processes (automata), have each reserve a data socket, and then pass the socket names so the two servers can connect to each other. The RFC calls this a useful general model and suggests that, if applied everywhere, the user/server distinction could vanish.

It endorses the model but proposes a more symmetrical approach: remove the requirement that the FTP user listen on the data socket first, replace LSTN with a new GETSocket command that returns a (send, receive) pair of socket numbers, have the user send those numbers to the opposite hosts with SOCK commands, and let each server issue an RFC containing the two socket numbers when it receives a transfer command.
sections.eli5: To send a file between two other computers, a go-between asks each for a mailbox number, trades the numbers, and tells them to talk directly.

sections.title: Site-Dependent Parameters
sections.content:
Some hosts, notably IBM systems, need extra file-system parameters that FTP cannot express. CCN first tried choosing a default mapping for each combination of type, mode and structure, but abandoned it for reasons that include too few distinct combinations, hard-to-remember rules, and non-invertible transformations such as truncating records to 80 bytes.

CCN decided on friendly defaults that store any FTP input invertibly (except print files), plus keywords on STOR such as "SOURCE" or "FORT", and fuller "DD" parameters for advanced users. The keywords would go in a generalized pathname. Alternatives are Hathaway's ALLO command or a server-dependent command sent through his proposed SRVR.
sections.eli5: Some big computers are picky about how a file is stored. The fix proposed is to let you add little hints to the file name.
